doc.title: Wilson "Chembo" Corniel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: Religion and the ceremonial batá drums
summary: Batá drums are consecrated; he describes initiation, the saint in the drum, Orisha songs, and how his religion informs his playing.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Does a spiritual aspect of this music enter as a part of your —
Oh yeah, yeah. Part of my religion also, yes.
I know it was talked about a lot yesterday.

Yeah. Those batá drums are ceremonial drums that we play at ceremonies, at religious ceremonies, and you have to go through a certain procedure in order to be able to touch those drums, the authentic ceremonial drums. So we go through a whole ceremony to get initiated to play those drums, like people who play those, because they have consecrated drums that are only used for these ceremonies. You know you could have the ones that we played yesterday, those are considered like conga drums, like any other, you could buy them in the store or on line, but the original ones that are done, like Cascadu said, they are tied up by rope or string or skin. They have a packet inside of the big one, like a medicine with herbs and everything like that. It’s a packet. That’s where the saint lives in the big one you know. And that one has to go through the ceremonies in order for them to be played by the sons of that saint, which we have to go through the ceremony and be initiated as omo ana, you know, which is the child of that saint, to touch the drum there. So you know, that’s, my religion is the religion of my drum. So this is why, if you’re going to go you’ve got to go all the way, you’ve got to learn my music, you know, I’m all the way, you have to learn where it came from to know where you’re going. So therefore with that, and it’s a whole total different thing. Now we’re playing, you see it as six drums, two, four, six, each side of the batá drum. He could be playing in 6/8, him in 4/4 and me in 2. And yet meshing into one. And then the conversations those calls, you know

it takes years of study to sing, and to each Orisha has a song and it’s in order, I think it’s about 23, 24, between 23 and 26 Orishas, and within each song there might be four or five conversations you know. And then there’s chants on top of that that sings to specific songs, so you can’t sing this song with that rhythm, it doesn’t go there. So you’ve got to know the rhythm, what it is, what is it for, which conversation are you singing it for, you can’t sing this one back onto this conversation. You know so it’s a lifetime thing. So that makes me understand my drum. When I go sit down and play drum I have all that power behind me you know. I have all that knowledge and right away if I just have one drum that’s what is going to come out because I know every square inch of that drum, where is it coming from, what I have to play, you know, so within my whole experience of my whole lifetime so far, and I’m still learning. This is why I’m glad that I was raised in New York, like I have all those influences, and it made you — you had to learn it because the guy next to you is learning it and he’s going to get the gig or whatever, you know, and if you stay back there — but this gives me another avenue also, besides playing, to teach.
